Stage 3 · Grammar

A reported question is not a question any more

Which is why it stops behaving like one.

Read what she asked, and what you would say afterwards.
  • “Did you enjoy it?”
  • He asked her whether she had enjoyed it.
What has happened to the word order?
A reported question is no longer a question. It is a statement about one.

This is the single idea the whole lesson rests on. When you report a question, you are not asking anything — you are telling somebody what was asked. The sentence is therefore a statement, and it behaves like one: no inversion, no auxiliary do, and no question mark.

That produces three changes on top of the normal reported-speech shifts. The word order returns to statement order, with the subject in front of the verb. Any do, does or did disappears completely — it is not moved elsewhere, it is deleted, because its only job was to build the direct question. And the tenses shift back exactly as they did in Lesson 34.

So ‘Where do you live?’ becomes She asked me where I lived. The sentence She asked me where did I live is such a recognisable error because it is trying to be two things at once: a statement in its function and a question in its shape.

Yes/no questions have a further problem: they contain no question word to introduce the reported clause. English supplies one, if or whether. ‘Are you free?’ becomes She asked if I was free. The two are usually interchangeable, but only whether can stand directly before or not. Finally, note that reporting a request uses a different structure altogether: ask + somebody + to + base verb.

Before you look at the table: the table below pairs each direct question with its reported form. Look specifically at what happens to do / does / did in every pair — that is the rule to internalise.

No that after ask. Not He asked me that if I was ready but He asked me if I was ready. That belongs with reported statements, not reported questions.

Full grammar reference — reported questions

What it is

A reported question tells somebody what was asked, without reproducing the question form. Two things change beyond the normal reported-speech shifts: the word order returns to statement order, and any do / does / did disappears. Yes/no questions additionally need if or whether, because they have no question word of their own.

What it means, and what it does

The point learners must internalise is that a reported question is no longer a question — it is a statement about a question. That is why it takes no inversion and no question mark. She asked what did I think is a very audible error precisely because the sentence is still trying to be two things at once.

When and why we use it

This is the single idea the whole lesson rests on. When you report a question, you are not asking anything — you are telling somebody what was asked. The sentence is therefore a statement, and it behaves like one: no inversion, no auxiliary do, and no question mark.

That produces three changes on top of the normal reported-speech shifts. The word order returns to statement order, with the subject in front of the verb. Any do, does or did disappears completely — it is not moved elsewhere, it is deleted, because its only job was to build the direct question. And the tenses shift back exactly as they did in Lesson 34.

So ‘Where do you live?’ becomes She asked me where I lived. The sentence She asked me where did I live is such a recognisable error because it is trying to be two things at once: a statement in its function and a question in its shape.

Yes/no questions have a further problem: they contain no question word to introduce the reported clause. English supplies one, if or whether. ‘Are you free?’ becomes She asked if I was free. The two are usually interchangeable, but only whether can stand directly before or not. Finally, note that reporting a request uses a different structure altogether: ask + somebody + to + base verb.

Typical situations

You need this for describing an interview or a meeting, telling somebody what you were asked, reporting a survey or a conversation, and softening your own questions in professional writing (I wondered whether…).

  • Reporting a wh- question — the question word stays and introduces the clause.She asked me why I had applied.
  • Reporting a yes/no question — if or whether replaces the missing question word.He wanted to know whether the hotel was open in winter.
  • Reporting a request — ask + object + to + base verb.She asked me to send the file again.
  • Reporting an offer or suggestion — the verb carries the function.He offered to help. · She suggested meeting earlier.
  • Softening your own question — the same structure used politely in the present.I wondered whether you had a moment.
  • Reporting a question you could not answer — common in interviews and stories.They asked me how long I had been in the job, and I couldn’t remember.

How it differs from similar structures

Direct: ‘What do you want?’ · Reported: She asked what I wanted. Three changes: no do, statement order, tense back one step.
ask somebody if / what… = report a question · ask somebody to… = report a request. He asked me if I could help vs He asked me to help.

How to build it

Wh- question: reporting verb (+ object) + wh-word + subject + verb (shifted back)
Yes/no question: reporting verb (+ object) + if / whether + subject + verb (shifted back)
Request: ask + somebody + to + base verb  ·  ask + somebody + not to + base verb
No do / does / did, no inversion, no question mark
Wh- question‘Where do you live?’ → She asked me where I lived.
Yes/no question‘Are you free?’ → She asked if I was free.
With whether‘Do you agree?’ → He asked whether I agreed.
Past question‘Did you see it?’ → She asked if I had seen it.
With will‘Will you come?’ → He asked if I would come.
Request‘Please wait.’ → She asked me to wait.
Negative request‘Don’t tell anyone.’ → He asked me not to tell anyone.
Reporting verbsask, want to know, wonder, enquire, be curious about
PunctuationFull stop, not a question mark: She asked where I lived.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The word order is the whole lesson. Subject before verb, exactly as in a statement: where I lived, never where did I live. This is the same rule as the indirect questions in Lesson 12.
  • Do / does / did vanish completely — they are not moved, they are deleted, because their only job was to form the question.
  • If and whether are usually interchangeable, but only whether works directly before or not and before to + verb: whether or not to apply.
  • Ask is the default reporting verb. Want to know and wonder are equally common in speech and slightly less formal.
  • A reported question never takes a question mark, even when the whole sentence reports a question. The exception is when the reporting sentence is itself a question: Did she ask where I lived?
  • The same tense-shift, pronoun and time rules from Lesson 34 apply on top of the word-order change. There are two jobs to do, not one.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • She asked me what did I think. → She asked me what I thought.Delete did and use statement word order.
  • He asked was I free on Friday. → He asked if I was free on Friday.A yes/no question needs if or whether.
  • She asked me where do I live. → She asked me where I lived.No auxiliary, and the tense shifts back.
  • He asked me that I would come. → He asked me if I would come.That reports a statement; a question takes if / whether.
  • She asked where I lived? → She asked where I lived.A reported question takes no question mark.
  • He asked to me to wait. → He asked me to wait.Ask takes the object directly.

More examples in context

  • wh- questionThe interviewer asked me why I had applied for the position.
  • wh- questionShe wanted to know how long I had been working there.
  • yes/noHe asked if I was willing to travel.
  • yes/no, formalThey enquired whether I had any management experience.
  • past questionShe asked whether I had seen the advert online.
  • with willHe asked if I would be able to start in September.
  • requestThe manager asked me to send my CV again.
  • negative requestShe asked me not to mention the salary.
  • softened own questionI wondered whether you had had a chance to look at my application.
  • reported and answeredThey asked me what my greatest weakness was, and I said honesty.

A tip for remembering it

Convert in three moves, in this order, every time. 1 Delete do / does / did. 2 Put the subject in front of the verb. 3 Shift the tense back one step. Then, if there was no question word, add if or whether at the front — and finish with a full stop, not a question mark.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. A reported question is a statement, so it takes statement word order and no question mark.
  2. Delete do / does / did — they are not moved, they disappear.
  3. Yes/no questions need if or whether; use whether before or not.
  4. The wh- word stays and introduces the clause.
  5. Tenses, pronouns and time words shift exactly as in reported speech.
  6. Ask somebody to + base verb reports a request, not a question.

11a · Read the whole text first. Then choose the form that fits each gap.

Researchers who study persuasion tend to say the same dull thing: the fastest way to change somebody’s mind is to stop talking. In one experiment, canvassers were told to knock on doors and ask people about a local issue. They were also told to ask in the household had ever changed their mind about it. Half the canvassers then argued their case; the other half simply asked that way, and listened. Three months later, researchers went back and asked residents . The listeners had produced a shift roughly ten times larger. One canvasser said she had been amazed she had needed to say. When the team was asked , the answer was one line: people are far more interested their own reasons than in yours.

Stage 5 · Main input

How to change someone’s mind

The people who are best at it are the ones who talk least.

Before you read: researchers have tested what actually changes somebody’s mind.

Which do you think works best?

Choose one. Paragraphs A and C give the research answer.

How to change someone's mind

Almost everything we instinctively do in an argument makes the other person less likely to agree. The research on this is unusually consistent, and unusually ignored.

AAsk people how to win an argument and most will describe the same method: gather the strongest facts, present them clearly, and wait for the other side to see sense. Researchers who study persuasion asked whether this works. In several studies, giving people accurate information that contradicted a firmly held belief produced no change at all, and in some cases the belief grew stronger. The listeners had not failed to understand the evidence. They had understood it and defended themselves against it.

BOne reason is that beliefs are rarely stored on their own. A view about a political question is usually attached to a group of people, a set of experiences and a sense of who you are. Attack the view directly and the person hears something larger being attacked, so they do what anybody does under attack: they hold on harder. This is why an argument between two well-informed people so often ends with both of them more certain than when they started.

CSo what does work? The most striking evidence comes from a technique in which trained volunteers knock on doors and, instead of arguing, ask questions. They ask whether the person has ever known anybody in the situation being discussed. Then they listen, without correcting anything, for ten or fifteen minutes. In controlled trials this approach produced measurable shifts in opinion that were still there weeks later — far more than a leaflet full of facts achieved.

DProfessional negotiators arrived at something similar from a different direction. One of them, who has spent his career teaching this, says that people ask him how to overcome objections and are disappointed by his answer. You do not overcome an objection, he tells them; you make sure the other person believes you have understood it. He advises repeating the objection back in your own words and asking whether you have got it right, and he claims that people will often argue themselves halfway towards you while you are still listening.

EThere is a warning attached to all of this. The techniques that genuinely change minds are the same ones used by people whose intentions are not good, and they work faster on those who are tired, frightened or alone. Nothing in the research says that a mind changed by careful listening has been changed towards the truth. It says only that it has been changed — which is a reason to notice when it is happening to you.

FWhat almost nobody wants to hear is how slow the honest version is. A leaflet costs pennies and reaches thousands. A conversation costs twenty minutes and reaches one person. Every organisation that has to persuade people at scale is aware of this arithmetic, and most of them choose the leaflet, knowing what the evidence says. Persuasion, it turns out, is not difficult to understand. It is difficult to afford.

Written for this course. Based on published work on persuasion and attitude change, including studies of the backfire effect and of deep canvassing.

1 · Work in pairs. The five-question rule.
Student A — you disagree

Pick something you and your partner see differently — a film, a city, a rule at work. You may not make a single statement of your own position. You may only ask questions. Five of them.

Student B — you hold the view

Answer honestly. At the end, say whether anything moved — and if so, which question did it.

Then swap roles. Notice how much harder it is to ask than to argue.
